title: Map of Anything
story: You've used Map[Str,Int] for name-to-score. But a Map can map ANY key type to ANY value type. You could map user IDs (Int) to names (Str), product codes (Str) to availability (Bool), or coordinates to terrain types. Your imagination is the limit.
why: Map[K,V] is doubly generic — recognizing this lets you model diverse real-world relationships: Int→Str, Str→Bool, Int→Float64, and custom types.
analogy: A Map[K,V] is like a filing cabinet with customizable labels. You choose what goes on the tab (K — Int for numbered files, Str for alphabetical) and what goes inside (V — Str for names, Bool for yes/no flags). The cabinet works the same regardless of the labeling system you choose.
try_it: Create a Map[Int,Float64] that maps student IDs to their GPA. Create a Map[Str,Vec[Str]] where each key (a category) maps to a Vec of items in that category. Write a generic `print_map[K,V]` function that takes a Map and a Vec of keys and prints each key-value pair.
tips: `Map[K,V]` means K and V can be any types — they're independent of each other
Common patterns: Map[Str,Int] for names to counts, Map[Int,Str] for IDs to names, Map[Str,Bool] for feature flags
Get and contains take the same type as K — a `Map[Int,Str]` expects Int keys, a `Map[Str,Bool]` expects Str keys
common_mistakes: Mixing up key and value positions: `Map[Int,Str]` means Int keys, Str values — not the other way around
Using the wrong key type with `.get()`: on a `Map[Int,Str]`, `.get("hello")` is a type error — must be `.get(42)`
Expecting Map to iterate in key order — Map doesn't guarantee any particular order
